dailyRead: The single most important thing today is that the trade which drove this entire week has stopped working, and it stopped for a reason you can name. All week metals were being sold not because anyone changed their mind about gold or copper, but because investors liquidating losing AI positions needed cash to cover them - TradingEconomics says so directly, that gold and silver came under pressure as declines in equity markets prompted investors to liquidate positions to cover losses in other assets. That forced selling has now stopped. Gold is 3,643.69 and up 2.15%, silver 44.03 and up 1.49%, and copper is 5.60 and up 4.40%, the biggest single move on this board. Every Asian market open today rose: the Nikkei was up 1.17% at 58,172 in the Tokyo lunch break, the Hang Seng 0.89% and the Kospi 2.72%. Europe closed higher on Thursday with the DAX up 0.66% and the Euro Stoxx 50 up 0.72%, and the Dow is up 4.72% on the week. Note what that does to the board: it is not a risk rally that lifts everything, it is a specific unwind that pays commodity currencies and takes the premium out of havens. The Aussie is the strongest currency here for a third session running. AUD/USD is 0.66705 and up 0.45%, AUD/JPY up 0.53%, AUD/CHF up 0.53% and AUD/CAD up 0.48%, and copper at plus 4.40% is the cleanest confirmation yet of Wednesday's argument - what sold copper 15.80% in a month was the market pricing an end to AI capital spending, and Australian Q3 capex rising 12.2% with information media and telecommunications investment up 86.7% to a record on data centres was direct evidence against it. Yesterday I corrected the Aussie short; today the correction is being paid. The honest hole in the Aussie is still there and it got bigger: the November composite PMI is 46.1, which is contraction, unemployment is at a four-year high of 4.9% after employment fell 43,531, and TradingEconomics still forecasts a hold at 4.85% on December 8. So the Aussie is being bought on prices and capital spending while its domestic activity data deteriorates, which is why this is a MEDIUM and not a HIGH. The yen is the mirror image and it has a hard new fact. Tokyo core CPI came in at 2.9% against a 3.0% forecast and 2.6% previously - a 16-month high, so the headline reads hawkish, but the composition does not. The entire acceleration is energy: energy inflation jumped from 2.2% to 9.5% because the government's electricity and gas subsidies expired, with electricity up 9.5% and city gas up 13.7%. Core-core, which strips fresh food and energy, actually eased to 2.5% from 2.6%. That is imported, temporary and precisely not what the Bank of Japan hikes on. December 17 to 18 stays above 85% priced and should still happen, but the January follow-up that board member Tamura floated on Wednesday - rates must reach neutral soon, neutral near 2% - just lost its evidence. Add a risk regime that has no use for a haven and Brent at 97.44 hitting the largest oil importer of the eight, and the yen is the weakest currency on this board. Every yen cross is higher. The franc is the other casualty, and this is where I have to mark my own position down. The franc has been scored positive all week on a haven bid, and the haven bid is exactly what came out today: AUD/CHF is up 0.53%, NZD/CHF up 0.31%, GBP/CHF up 0.08% and EUR/CHF up 0.04%. With the policy rate at zero, core inflation at 0.5% and the SNB forecast to hold on December 10, there is nothing underneath it. So the franc goes from plus one to minus one, and the only franc long I will keep is against the euro, for a dated reason given below. The dollar's problem is now three failures deep. Core PCE and a 4.3% Q3 GDP revision on Wednesday did not lift it. December pricing moving to between 97% and 99% on CME FedWatch did not lift it. And overnight the 10-year went back up to about 4.904%, a rise of five basis points, and DXY still slipped to 103.693, down 0.10%. A currency that cannot rally on hawkish data, near-certain pricing and rising yields has finished trading December, so the dollar comes down from plus one to zero and everything now waits on the dot plot at 21:00 on December 9, with January 2027 priced at about 72.5%. The euro is in the same priced-out trap with a dated risk attached. Thursday's ECB accounts were hawkish on the past - a large share of policymakers were ready to hike back in October and only delayed to collect more inflation evidence, and the accounts said a hike then would simply have frontloaded the necessary tightening - and December 17 is now described as all but done and fully priced to 2.75%. But the same accounts noted inflation has not generated dangerous second-round effects and that energy prices had retreated, which is the language that caps anything beyond December. Meanwhile S&P delivers its verdict on France's A+ rating today, with economists split between a downgrade to A and a milder outlook cut, Moody's already at Aa3 negative, and French prelim CPI at 09:45 and Spanish flash CPI at 10:00 both forecast lower than the prior month. That is a one-way risk into a long weekend. Sterling is the one currency where I think the market is missing something concrete. Ofgem confirmed on Wednesday that the energy price cap rises 26% to 2,166 pounds from 1 January, adding about 443 pounds to the bills of 20 million households, and Ofgem blamed the Middle East conflict for roughly tripling global gas prices. Bailey, Lombardelli and Mann have all said that unless Middle East tensions ease and energy prices fall sharply the Bank must respond with policy - and energy has not fallen sharply, it has risen, with Brent up and EU gas back above 88 euros on cold weather and weak wind generation. That condition has failed, the Bank already forecasts inflation near 5% by the middle of next year, and December 17 prices at 80% to 82% with some measures at 89%. Against it: 64 of 65 economists expect a hold, and sterling made a 19-month low of 1.3011 on November 23 and is down about 2% in November, trading 1.31249 now. So sterling is hawkish and unpaid, which has been a trap all month - but the cap rise is a hard number the rate market has not finished digesting. The Canadian dollar keeps a good story and still lost ground, which is the most useful thing on the board today. WTI is 86.30 and up 1.62%, on track for its first weekly rise in four weeks, Brent is 97.44, and December 9 prices between 72% on Kalshi and 80% on LSEG. And yet AUD/CAD rose 0.48% and NZD/CAD 0.26%: on a day when both commodities rose, copper beat crude. The loonie is therefore still a buy against the euro, sterling and the yen, but not against the other commodity currencies - and note one correction, because yesterday's file said CIBC saw a second consecutive hike while current reporting has CIBC expecting a December hold and a January move. Macklem named next week's Q3 GDP and November labour force survey as the deciders and they still are. The kiwi comes up from minus one to zero and I want to be clear why, because it is not the 0.26% it gained today. Two real things changed: the RBNZ's October hold was a 4-3 split with Gourley, Conway and Silk already voting for 3.00%, and oil rising about 6% since Monday is precisely the near-term inflation pressure the bank's chief economist named, alongside a weaker currency. ActionForex and UOB both call a 25 basis point move to 3.00% on December 9 and one preview puts a hold at only about 10%. Against that stands the weakest labour market of the eight at 5.7% unemployment with private wage growth of 2.0%, which is why this is zero and not positive. The two European indices have swapped places from yesterday and EU50 deserves its own note, because yesterday I had it short on the periphery and the banks leading Wednesday's selloff. It outperformed the DAX today, up 0.72% against 0.66%, the AI liquidation that drove that periphery and bank selling has stopped, and a steeper curve with a hawkish ECB helps banks, which are its heaviest sector. So the EU50 short comes out and both indices become ranges - EU50 because the France decision lands today, GER40 because gas back above 88 euros is a direct German industrial cost even while the risk-on leg wins. Last, the trading conditions, which matter more than usual. Today is the Black Friday half session: the NYSE and Nasdaq open at 16:30 and close at 20:00, with bond markets shutting at 21:00, there are no red folders anywhere on the calendar for the eight currencies, and the only US releases are a goods trade balance and wholesale inventories at 15:30. Thin books plus no catalyst means a handful of large orders can push a pair well past where the fundamentals put it, and it means any level that breaks today deserves less trust than usual. Size down, take the cleanest expressions - long AUD/JPY, long copper, short EUR/AUD - and do not chase a move you cannot explain.

USD.when: December 9 at 21:00 with a new dot plot, and the quarter point is 97% to 99% priced
USD.note: TradingEconomics carries the Fed funds rate at 4.00% as the upper bound of the 3.75% to 4.00% range, held on October 28 with two policymakers voting for a 25 basis point hike. CME FedWatch has moved up again, to between 97% and 99% from 94% to 98% yesterday, with a larger half-point move now at zero and January 2027 priced near 72.5%; a hike takes the range to 4.00% to 4.25%. Wednesday's data was hawkish on every line the Worker recorded - core PCE 0.3% m/m in line and the second estimate of Q3 GDP revised up to 4.3% against a 3.5% forecast - and TradingEconomics carries headline CPI at 3.7% for September with core CPI at 2.6%. The tradeable point is what the dollar did with all of it: nothing. It failed to rally on the data, failed on the move to near-certain pricing, and failed again overnight when the 10-year rose about five basis points to roughly 4.904%, with DXY slipping to 103.693. December is therefore finished as a trade and the dot plot does all the work, because November CPI only lands on December 10. Today is the Black Friday half session: the cash market runs 16:30 to 20:00 and bonds close at 21:00.

EUR.when: December 17 at 15:15, now described as all but done and fully priced to 2.75%
EUR.note: TradingEconomics carries the deposit facility rate at 2.50%, with the main refinancing rate at 2.65% and the marginal lending rate at 2.90%, all held on October 29. Thursday's accounts of that meeting were the new information and they cut both ways. Hawkish on the past: a large share of policymakers were already prepared to hike in October and only delayed to gather more evidence on inflation risks, and the accounts recorded that moving then would simply have frontloaded the necessary tightening. Capping on the future: the same accounts noted inflation has not generated dangerous second-round effects and that energy prices had retreated, which is the language that makes anything beyond December non-urgent, and ING argues further 2027 hikes would do more harm than good. Euro-area inflation is 4.0%, a three-year high, with core at 2.6%. The energy input has swung again - EU gas is 87.47 euros and TradingEconomics reports it back above 88 euros today on colder weather and weak wind generation, with below-normal temperatures expected until about December 10, while Brent is 97.44. The split is unchanged: German composite PMI 55.0 against a French composite at 46.2. Today carries the dated risk - S&P rules on France's A+ rating, French prelim CPI is at 09:45 with the monthly forecast at minus 0.2%, Spanish flash CPI at 10:00 is forecast 4.7% from 4.9%, German unemployment change at 10:55 and Nagel speaks at 14:40. Lagarde steps down on February 7, 2027.

GBP.when: December 17 at 14:00, priced 80% to 82% and up to 89% on some measures, against 64 of 65 economists at a hold
GBP.note: TradingEconomics carries Bank Rate at 4.00% after the November 5 quarter-point rise from 3.75%, with the vote 8-1 and Catherine Mann wanting fifty basis points to 4.25%. The new fact this week is Ofgem: the energy price cap rises 26% to 2,166 pounds from 1 January, about 443 pounds more a year for the 20 million households on standard variable tariffs, and Ofgem attributes it to the Middle East conflict roughly tripling global gas prices. That matters because of the condition the Bank set itself - Bailey, Lombardelli and Mann have all said that unless Middle East tensions ease and energy prices fall sharply the Bank must respond with policy, and energy has not fallen sharply but risen, with Brent at 97.44 and EU gas back above 88 euros. Megan Greene has said further tightening would be appropriate. The Bank already expects inflation to reach around 5% by the middle of next year. TradingEconomics has CPI at 3.6% with core steady at 2.8%, unemployment improved to 4.6%, annual growth 1.9% and employment change plus 156,000, with wage growth slowing to 3.6% from 3.8%. Pricing is 80% on LSEG, 82% on one FXStreet read and as high as 89% after recent speeches, while a Reuters poll found 64 of 65 economists expecting a hold and 4.25% the peak. Sterling is the problem: a 19-month low of 1.3011 on November 23, down about 2% in November, trading 1.31249 now. Nothing is scheduled for the United Kingdom today.

JPY.when: December 17 to 18, with the decision at 05:00 Friday December 18 to 1.50%, above 85% priced
JPY.note: TradingEconomics carries the policy rate at 1.25% after the October 30 hold, an 8-1 vote with Hajime Takata dissenting for faster hikes, and its calendar forecasts 1.50% for December. Tokyo core CPI this morning at 01:30 is the new evidence and it argues against the January extension rather than against December. Core rose to 2.9% from 2.6%, a 16-month high, but below the 3.0% consensus - and the composition is the story. Energy inflation jumped from 2.2% in October to 9.5% in November because the government's electricity and gas subsidy payments ended, with electricity up 9.5% and city gas up 13.7% year on year. Headline edged to 2.8% from 2.7%. Core-core, excluding fresh food and energy, eased to 2.5% from 2.6%. So the acceleration is an imported, administered, one-off energy effect while the underlying measure softened, which is not what the Bank tightens on. December should still happen - a Reuters poll of 71 economists had 61 expecting the quarter point - but the January follow-up that board member Tamura floated on Wednesday, when he said rates must reach neutral soon and put neutral near 2%, has lost its supporting data. Wage growth at 4.6% is still the fastest of the eight and core CPI is 2.2%. Two things cap the yen regardless: the Fed moves first on December 9, with the US 10-year near 4.904% against a Japanese 10-year around 2.71%; and Brent at 97.44 is a direct terms-of-trade hit to the biggest oil importer here. Spot at 159.332 has not closed above 160.00 since September 1 nor traded above 160.50 since the July 31 joint intervention. Nationwide November CPI lands on December 18, the same day as the decision.

AUD.when: December 8 at 05:30, where TradingEconomics still carries 4.85% and only about 45% of a hike is priced
AUD.note: TradingEconomics carries the cash rate at 4.85% after the November 3 rise from 4.60%, an 18-year high and the fifth increase of 2026, and still forecasts 4.85% for December 8. The price data keeps surprising one way. October CPI beat on all three red-folder lines - headline 4.9% against 4.7% from 4.3%, monthly 0.5% against 0.4%, trimmed mean monthly 0.5% against 0.3% - with trimmed mean at 3.8% y/y, and Q3 private capital expenditure then rose 12.2% against a 4.4% forecast, the largest quarterly rise since 2011, with equipment and machinery up 23.1%, information media and telecommunications up 86.7% to a record on data-centre spending and 2026-27 plans revised up 11.8% to 223.7 billion dollars. Today copper at 5.60 and up 4.40% is the market agreeing with that read. But the activity side is deteriorating and this is the honest counterweight: the November composite PMI is 46.1, down from 48.2 and firmly in contraction, unemployment is at a four-year high of 4.9% after employment fell 43,531, and wage growth is 3.5%. ANZ and Westpac still expect a hold and one tracker prices about 45% of a hike, so the policy call has not changed - the Aussie is being bought on prices, commodities and capital spending while its domestic activity data weakens, which is why the conviction here is medium rather than high. Three of nine members opposed the November rise and the November minutes majority judged previous tightening was not clearly sufficient. Australia's Q3 GDP is due next week.

NZD.when: December 9 at 03:00 with a Monetary Policy Statement, where TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00%
NZD.note: TradingEconomics carries the Official Cash Rate at 2.75% after the October 28 hold, which surprised a market priced near 90% for a rise, and forecasts 3.00% for December 9. Two things have firmed the hike case and they are the reason the kiwi comes off the bottom of this board. First, that October hold was a 4-3 split: Breman, Hansen, Williams and Gai voted to hold while Gourley, Conway and Silk already voted for 3.00%, so one vote decides it. Second, oil has risen about 6% since Monday's three-month low and that is exactly the near-term inflation pressure the bank's chief economist named, alongside a weaker New Zealand dollar. ActionForex and UOB both expect a 25 basis point move to 3.00% on December 9, with one preview putting a hold at only about 10%, though BNZ cautions it is not a done deal and depends on fuel prices, inflation expectations and second-round pricing. The November Survey of Expectations supports them, with respondents at 3.05% by the end of the December quarter and 3.40% in a year, and one-year inflation expectations up to 2.92% from 2.60%. Against all of it sits the weakest labour market of the eight: unemployment 5.7%, the highest since 2016, employment down 0.1% on the quarter and private wage growth 2.0%, the lowest here. Q3 CPI fell to 3.7% from 4.1% with core steady at 3.2%, while annual growth improved to 2.6%. There is no New Zealand release before December 9.

CAD.when: December 9 at 16:45, priced between 72% on Kalshi and 80% on LSEG
CAD.note: TradingEconomics carries the overnight rate at 2.50% after the October 28 rise from 2.25%, the first increase in three years, and forecasts 2.75% for December 9. Pricing has settled into a range rather than a single number: Kalshi about 72%, Polymarket 76%, LSEG 79% to 80%, after Macklem's Toronto remarks to the Economic Club of Canada where he reaffirmed the 2% target, admitted the Bank had sent mixed messages on core inflation and repeated that he expects firms to pass higher costs through in the coming months. One correction to yesterday's file: current reporting has CIBC expecting a December hold and a January hike, not a second consecutive move, while separately all six of Canada's largest banks were reported to expect a December increase - the two accounts conflict and both are in the market. The oil concession Macklem gave himself has been overtaken: WTI is 86.30 and up 1.62%, on track for its first weekly rise in four weeks, which removes the disinflation argument and adds a terms-of-trade tailwind for the only net energy exporter of the eight. The soft side is unchanged and real: core CPI 2.0%, trimmed 1.8%, median 2.0%, headline 3.1%, unemployment 6.7%, employment down 4,700 in October and a composite PMI of 48.1 in contraction. Macklem named next week's Q3 GDP and November labour force survey as the deciders and they still carry the meeting. Current account today at 15:30 is the only item, forecast 9.5 billion from 8.8 billion.

CHF.note: TradingEconomics carries the SNB policy rate at 0.00%, held on September 24 and unchanged since mid-2025, and forecasts 0.00% for December 10. At that meeting the bank said the current stance remains appropriate, noted inflation had risen on higher energy prices, forecast average inflation of 0.7% in 2026 and 0.8% in both 2027 and 2028 with GDP growth of 1.5% to 2% in 2026, and flagged high uncertainty from Middle East tensions, trade policy and exchange rates. It repeated that it remains willing to intervene in foreign exchange markets as necessary. October headline inflation is 1.5%, near a three-year high, but core is 0.5%, so the gap is imported energy rather than domestic pressure and the bank has nothing to respond to. The important change is not policy, it is the regime. The franc has been carried all week by a haven bid and that bid came out today: AUD/CHF is up 0.53%, NZD/CHF up 0.31%, GBP/CHF up 0.08% and EUR/CHF up 0.04%, with USD/CHF at 0.83404 only because the dollar is the weaker leg. With nothing to hike on and no haven premium, the franc trades on the risk regime and on the intervention cap, and the only franc long worth keeping is against the euro, where S&P rules on France's A+ rating today. There is no Swiss release left this week.

catalysts.note: At 23:00. The speech that set the week up: more hikes likely over time to return inflation to 2%, the AI investment boom could force further tightening in 2027, and only dramatic action ruled out. December went from about 88% to near certainty and has since reached 97% to 99%.

catalysts.event: Euro-area, German and French flash PMIs
catalysts.note: At 10:15. German composite 55.0, the highest since March 2022, against a French composite at 46.2 contracting fastest since May; the aggregate held 51.7. The two-speed problem is still the live euro risk and is why GER40 and EU50 are scored separately.
At 17:00. Printed 103.3 against a 92.4 forecast and 91.7 previous - a very large beat that fed the rotation into Dow value names and still underpins the index three sessions later.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada Governor Macklem speaks
catalysts.note: At 19:25. At the Economic Club of Canada he reaffirmed the 2% target, admitted past mixed messaging on core inflation and repeated that firms will pass costs through, while conceding oil could pull inflation below forecast. December 9 moved to roughly 80% on LSEG. The oil concession has since been overtaken by WTI at 86.30.

At 02:30. Above forecast on all three red-folder lines, with TradingEconomics putting trimmed mean at 3.8% y/y. Read with Wednesday's capex beat and today's 4.40% copper move, it is the third one-way Australian signal of the week.

Rose 12.2% against a 4.4% forecast, the largest quarterly rise since 2011, with equipment and machinery up 23.1% and information media and telecommunications up 86.7% to a record on data-centre spending; 2026-27 plans revised up 11.8% to 223.7 billion dollars. The evidence that AI capital spending is not stopping.

catalysts.event: US October core PCE and prelim Q3 GDP
catalysts.note: At 15:30. Hawkish on both lines the Worker recorded, and the dollar could not use it - the first of three straight failures to rally. December pricing has since moved to 97% to 99% on CME FedWatch.

catalysts.event: Ofgem raises the UK energy price cap 26%
catalysts.note: The cap rises to 2,166 pounds from 1 January, about 443 pounds more a year for the 20 million households on standard variable tariffs, with Ofgem attributing it to the Middle East conflict roughly tripling global gas prices. The hard number behind the sterling hawkish case, and the reason the Bank's own energy condition has failed.

catalysts.event: Houthi strike claimed on Ras Tanura refinery
catalysts.note: The Houthis said they hit Saudi Arabia's largest refinery and the coalition confirmed intercepting four drones without confirming a strike; NASA and Planet Labs imagery showed a large black smoke plume. A shipping source said loadings at the terminal were suspended and no resumption has been confirmed. Brent settled 3.5% higher that day and is 97.44 now.

At 01:50. Rose 4.2% y/y against a 3.6% forecast and 3.8% previous - the cleanest read on domestic rather than imported pressure, and the figure Tamura built his neutral-rate argument on. This morning's Tokyo core-core easing to 2.5% cuts the other way.

catalysts.event: ECB October monetary policy meeting accounts
catalysts.note: At 14:30. Hawkish on the past and capping on the future in one document: a large share of policymakers were already prepared to hike in October and delayed only to gather more inflation evidence, with the record noting a move then would simply have frontloaded the necessary tightening - but the accounts also noted inflation has not generated dangerous second-round effects and that energy had retreated. December 17 is now called all but done and fully priced to 2.75%.
Cash equities and bonds shut. European stocks rallied in the gap, tracking the rebound of the AI trade in North American futures, with the DAX up 0.66% and the Euro Stoxx 50 up 0.72%.

At 01:30. A 16-month high that misses the consensus, and the composition is the trade: energy inflation jumped from 2.2% to 9.5% as electricity and gas subsidies expired, with electricity up 9.5% and city gas up 13.7%, while core-core excluding fresh food and energy eased to 2.5% from 2.6% and headline edged to 2.8%. December stays above 85% priced; the January extension loses its evidence.

catalysts.event: French prelim CPI, GDP and consumer spending
catalysts.note: At 09:45. Monthly CPI forecast at minus 0.2% from 0.4%, prelim GDP at minus 0.1% and consumer spending at 0.1%. A soft set would undercut the euro on the same morning S&P rules on the rating.
At 10:00. Forecast 4.7% y/y from 4.9% - the first euro-area national print of the month and a downward one, against an aggregate rate at a three-year high of 4.0%.
At 10:55. Forecast 5,000 from 4,000. Minor, but it is the labour-market check on a German composite PMI running at its best since March 2022.
At 14:40. The first ECB voice after the accounts, into a market that already prices December 17 fully. Only tradeable if he pushes back on the accounts' no-second-round-effects language.

catalysts.event: Canada current account and US goods trade balance
catalysts.note: At 15:30. Canada's current account is forecast 9.5 billion from 8.8 billion, the only Canadian item this week; the US goods trade balance is forecast minus 135.9 billion with prelim wholesale inventories at 0.5%. The only releases of the US session.

catalysts.event: S&P ruling on France's A+ rating
catalysts.note: France goes in at A+ with a stable outlook and this date is published by the French debt agency. Economists are split: one calls a cut to A quite logical, BNP Paribas argues S&P is not obliged to move now and could revise only the outlook. Moody's holds Aa3 with a negative outlook and Fitch has moved to negative. A one-way euro and EU50 risk into a long weekend.

Cash equities open 16:30 and close 20:00 instead of 23:00, with bond markets shutting at 21:00. No red folders anywhere for the eight currencies. Thin books mean a handful of large orders can move a pair well past where the fundamentals put it - size down and distrust breaks.

At 05:30. TradingEconomics forecasts a hold at 4.85% and only about 45% of a hike is priced, with ANZ and Westpac both at a hold - despite CPI beating on all three lines and capex rising 12.2%. The November composite PMI at 46.1 and unemployment at a four-year high are why they stay put. Australia's Q3 GDP lands first.

catalysts.event: RBNZ Official Cash Rate and Monetary Policy Statement
catalysts.note: At 03:00. TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00% and ActionForex and UOB both expect the quarter point, with one preview putting a hold near 10%. The October hold was a 4-3 split with Gourley, Conway and Silk already voting to hike, so one vote decides it. Oil up about 6% since Monday is the pressure the chief economist named.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada overnight rate decision
catalysts.note: At 16:45. Priced between about 72% on Kalshi and 80% on LSEG for 2.75%. Macklem named next week's Q3 GDP and November labour force survey as the deciders, so those two releases carry this meeting rather than anything he says before it.

catalysts.event: Fed rate decision, dot plot and press conference
catalysts.note: At 21:00. The quarter point to a 4.00% to 4.25% range is 97% to 99% priced, so the decision is not the event - the Summary of Economic Projections is, because it is the first official read on 2027 and January already prices near 72.5%. The dollar has failed to rally on everything else, so this is where it gets resolved. November CPI follows on December 10.

At 10:30. TradingEconomics carries 0.00% and forecasts no change. With core inflation at 0.5% there is nothing to respond to; what matters is any repeat of the willingness to intervene in FX, which is the franc's real cap.

catalysts.event: Bank of England Bank Rate decision
catalysts.note: At 14:00. Priced 80% to 82% and up to 89% on some measures, against a Reuters poll finding 64 of 65 economists at a hold. Ofgem's 26% cap rise from January and the failure of the Bank's own energy condition are the hawkish case; the vote split after November's 8-1 is the thing to read.

catalysts.event: ECB deposit rate decision and press conference
catalysts.note: At 15:15. Fully priced to 2.75% and described as all but done. The trade is the guidance, because the October accounts noted no dangerous second-round effects and that energy had retreated - the language that makes 2027 non-urgent. Lagarde steps down on February 7, 2027.

At 05:00, with nationwide November CPI the same day. TradingEconomics forecasts 1.50% and 61 of 71 polled economists expect it, with the market above 85%. This morning's Tokyo core-core easing to 2.5% does not threaten December but does take the January follow-up Tamura floated off the table for now.

The transit story and the production story are now running together. Ras Tanura loadings were suspended after Wednesday's claimed strike with no confirmed resumption, Saudi Arabia is leaning on Yanbu to bypass the strait entirely, and the IRGC keeps claiming tanker mine strikes that UKMTO has not confirmed. WTI 86.30 and Brent 97.44, both on their first weekly rise in four weeks but still down 16.03% and 12.72% on the month.

geopolitics: Day 272 of a closed Strait of Hormuz, and the shape of the risk has changed again - this time in the direction of production rather than transit. The anchor event is Wednesday's claimed Houthi strike on Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, the kingdom's largest refinery and one of the largest in the world. The accounts still do not agree and it matters to say so precisely: Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the attack caused fires, the Saudi-led coalition said air defences intercepted and destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura and has never confirmed the refinery itself was hit, and against that, Reuters examined NASA and Planet Labs satellite imagery showing a substantial plume of black smoke above the industrial site on November 25. The extent of the damage has not been disclosed. The consequential detail is commercial rather than military: a shipping source told CNN that oil loadings at the terminal were suspended after the attack, and as of this morning no resumption has been confirmed - the reports of Ras Tanura loadings restarting that circulate in search results date from June, after the four-month Iranian blockade, not from this week. Saudi Arabia has meanwhile leaned more heavily on its Yanbu terminal on the Red Sea, where crude arrives through the East-West pipeline and can be exported without entering Hormuz at all, which is the single most important mitigating fact in the whole picture. Separately the IRGC Navy has again claimed tanker mine strikes inside the strait, and UKMTO has reported unidentified projectiles striking commercial ships near Dubai with crews accounted for but has not confirmed mines; that pattern of competing unverifiable claims has now run for five weekends and should be treated as background noise rather than new information. The market read: WTI is 86.30 and up 1.62%, Brent 97.44 and up 1.09%, and TradingEconomics has both on track for their first weekly rise in four weeks explicitly on attacks against Middle Eastern energy facilities and tankers. Keep the levels in perspective, because this is where the honest edge is - WTI is still down 16.03% on the month and Brent down 12.72%, even while WTI is up 47.40% and Brent up 56.21% on the year. The premium is rebuilding from a low base, not breaking out. The FX transmission runs four ways and all four are live today. First, the Canadian dollar is the only net energy exporter of the eight, so a firm crude price is a direct terms-of-trade tailwind and it removes the disinflation caveat Macklem gave himself in Toronto - which is why USD/CAD short and EUR/CAD short stay on. Second, the yen is the largest importer here and takes the hit from the other side, reinforcing a currency already weakened by this morning's Tokyo print, so CAD/JPY long is the cleanest two-sided energy expression on the board. Third, and this is the leg that is newly concrete, the United Kingdom has turned the energy shock into domestic policy: Ofgem raised the energy price cap 26% to 2,166 pounds from 1 January, adding about 443 pounds a year for 20 million households, and attributed it directly to the Middle East conflict roughly tripling global gas prices. Bailey, Lombardelli and Mann each said the Bank must respond with policy unless Middle East tensions ease and energy prices fall sharply, and with Brent at 97.44 and EU gas back above 88 euros that condition has plainly failed - so Hormuz is now a Bank of England story, not only an oil story. Fourth, Europe pays twice: EU gas at 87.47 euros is up 203.53% on the year and TradingEconomics reports it rising above 88 euros today on colder weather and weak wind generation, with below-normal temperatures expected across Germany and eastern Europe until about December 10, which is a direct industrial cost and the reason GER40 is capped at a range even on a risk-on day. The franc is the piece that did not behave today, and that is informative rather than contradictory: the franc's bid all week was a haven premium tied to the equity liquidation, not to Hormuz, so when the liquidation stopped the premium came out even though the war headlines did not improve. That tells you the market is pricing the AI unwind and the Middle East separately right now. The asymmetry for the week ahead: a confirmed resumption of Ras Tanura loadings takes the premium out quickly and would hurt long USOIL, long CAD and the sterling hawkish case together, while any strike that is confirmed to have damaged processing capacity rather than merely halting loadings is a step-change higher, because supply destruction is a bigger number than supply delay.
